stories.title: Orchestrating autonomous agents to decompile a first-person shooter
stories.social_post:
Scaling autonomous coding agents to decompile an entire binary requires treating the agent loop like an automated compiler toolchain.

Running multi-agent systems across five hundred billion tokens reveals that model choice matters far less than harness design. Giving autonomous agents unbounded context windows causes them to wander and hallucinate duplicate symbols. Effective execution demands deterministic feedback loops: feeding compiler errors, symbol tables, and test harness execution back into the agent context in tight cycles.

The orchestration system must treat each module decompilation as an isolated transaction. Breaking down disassembly into discrete functions with verified type signatures allows agents to make steady forward progress without polluting global state.

When orchestrating agents over months of continuous execution, strict verification boundaries beat raw model capability every single time.

Reliable agentic software engineering is an infrastructure problem, not a prompting exercise.
stories.why_read: Learn how to structure long-running agent harnesses, verify iterative machine code outputs, and avoid context bloat.

stories.title: Multi-agent collective intelligence enables recursive self-improvement in AI
stories.social_post:
Scaling language models on non-verifiable tasks cannot rely solely on human supervision, because human evaluation quickly becomes the core bottleneck. The MASS framework from Sakana AI and UC Berkeley tackles this limit by turning multi-agent collaboration into an automated training flywheel for recursive self-improvement.

Instead of treating agent workflows as mere prompt orchestration, the system executes multi-agent teams on complex research benchmarks, captures their collective problem-solving trajectories, and distills that shared execution trace back into the base model. This creates a closed-loop supervision signal where the model alternates between acting as the worker, the optimizer, and the evaluator.

The resulting feedback loop improves benchmark accuracy per generated token without needing expanding human evaluation budgets. For teams designing autonomous agent architectures, this demonstrates that multi-agent interactions are not just execution mechanisms, but high-density data generators for continuous model fine-tuning.

The future of agentic engineering lies in distilling multi-agent coordination traces directly into model weights.
stories.why_read: Explores how multi-agent workflows can generate training data for self-improving foundation models on research tasks.

stories.title: Solving SQLite's single-writer limitation without modifying source code
stories.social_post:
SQLite has powered trillions of client and embedded deployments, but its strict single-writer limitation has long constrained high-concurrency backend workloads. While write-ahead logging, batching queues, and busy timeouts alleviate lock contention, they cannot fundamentally eliminate the single write lock bottleneck.

Engineers frequently hit throughput walls when multiple background workers write to an embedded database concurrently. Because standard SQLite write transactions take an exclusive lock on the entire database file, concurrent operations force callers into serialization queues or busy handler retries.

Recent architecture work demonstrates that supporting concurrent multi-process writers does not require maintaining custom forks or rewriting the storage engine with multi-version concurrency control. By decoupling lock management and handling transaction coordination externally, systems can execute concurrent writes against standard, unmodified SQLite databases safely.

This architecture lets developers keep the operational simplicity of embedded databases without sacrificing concurrent write throughput.
stories.why_read: Understand the trade-offs of using external transaction managers to circumvent SQLite single-writer lock contention.

stories.title: Plimsoll reports verifiable isolation tiers for untrusted code
stories.social_post:
Running agent-generated code safely in production requires formal isolation guarantees, not wishful thinking. Plimsoll introduces a self-hosted sandbox system that models isolation strength through explicit execution tiers: process, container, kernel, and full virtual machine.

Instead of treating sandboxing as a binary setting, the engine tags every execution output with the verifiable boundary it ran behind. Callers can enforce a strict baseline threshold, ensuring that code automatically fails to execute if the required isolation tier is unavailable.

For teams deploying autonomous coding agents or code interpreter pipelines, this pattern solves the gap between agent tool autonomy and infrastructure security.
stories.why_read: Learn how to enforce minimum isolation guarantees like process, container, or microVM boundaries for AI agent sandboxes.

stories.title: Dynamic shredding of semi-structured JSON yields massive speedups
stories.social_post:
Querying semi-structured JSON at scale in log and trace systems is notoriously slow because engines must parse dynamic payloads row by row. Dynamic shredding solves this bottleneck by transparently decomposing repeated JSON attributes into typed columnar vectors at ingestion or compaction time.

Instead of repeatedly parsing nested variant trees during query execution, the storage engine extracts hot paths such as user identifiers or HTTP route strings into discrete columns. Cold or highly irregular fields remain in the fallback semi-structured blob. Logfire observed query times drop from thirty-second timeouts down to sub-second executions, achieving speedups of more than one thousand times.

This hybrid storage layout provides the developer agility of schema-free JSON alongside the scan throughput of columnar storage formats like Parquet. It completely avoids the operational friction of manual schema migrations while preserving vectorization and compression efficiency.

You do not need to choose between flexible schemas and fast analytical queries.
stories.why_read: Learn how dynamic shredding extracts hot JSON paths into typed columnar vectors to avoid row-by-row parsing overhead.

stories.title: Jointly training tool creation and use improves agent reasoning
stories.social_post:
Most tool-augmented large language models remain bottlenecked by the static interfaces written by human engineers. When researchers attempt to let models generate their own tools at inference time, the tool creator is usually decoupled from the tool consumer. This lack of feedback causes schema mismatches and invocation failures.

The SMITH framework resolves this decoupling by treating tool creation and tool execution as a unified reinforcement learning loop inside a single policy. Instead of freezing the model, rollouts alternate between authoring code based on examples and executing pooled tools on held-out reasoning problems. The optimization uses three independent reward axes to isolate schema definition errors, runtime code crashes, and incorrect task outcomes. Each failure mode produces targeted gradients back to the policy.

This dual optimization allows a compact four-billion parameter model to reach nearly eighty percent macro-average accuracy on unseen procedural tasks, surpassing untrained models an order of magnitude larger. Furthermore, tools generated by this policy generalize effectively to smaller frozen downstream models without schema degeneration.

Training models to use tools is useful, but teaching them to build the tools they consume changes the ceiling of agent autonomy.
stories.why_read: Learn how reinforcement learning loops can unify API creation and invocation within small language models.

stories.title: Containers fail as security boundaries making microVMs necessary
stories.social_post:
Linux containers are resource governance mechanisms rather than true security perimeters. Treating cgroups and namespaces as isolation walls for untrusted code execution is a recipe for catastrophic host compromise, as demonstrated by eight container escape vulnerabilities discovered within eighteen months.

The rise of untrusted AI agent execution makes hardware-level isolation non-negotiable. Modern microVM implementations, powered by the shared rust-vmm crate ecosystem, eliminate the historical latency penalties of traditional virtualization. Virtual machines built on hypervisors like Firecracker boot in approximately one hundred twenty-five milliseconds while consuming less than five megabytes of memory overhead.

Platforms running arbitrary agent-generated code must separate the host kernel from the execution target. MicroVMs provide this exact boundary without sacrificing density, making them the standard architectural primitive for multi-tenant sandboxes.

Fast isolation is no longer a luxury when models execute arbitrary code in production.
stories.why_read: Understand the hypervisor landscape, rust-vmm internals, and performance tradeoffs when running untrusted agent code in microVMs.

stories.title: Versioned filesystems provide transactional state for disposable execution sandboxes
stories.social_post:
Running untrusted code inside isolated gVisor sandboxes is straightforward until you need to persist and branch state between workflow steps. If every sandbox execution destroys its local state, developers lose the ability to inspect intermediate artifacts or run iterative tasks without paying massive serialization penalties.

The engineering team at Tines solved this by building a transactional, copy-on-write filesystem tailored specifically for disposable sandboxes. Each workflow step treats its filesystem operations like a database transaction: changes are committed as a new immutable snapshot only when the step completes successfully. If a step fails, the runtime discards the uncommitted snapshot entirely, preventing corrupted partial state.

By decoupling the commit metadata from block storage and tiering hot data on local disks with cold data in S3, sandboxes can branch off historical snapshots in milliseconds without duplicating underlying bytes. This architecture allows developers and autonomous agents to fork draft environments off production data without write conflicts.

Treating ephemeral filesystem state as versioned immutable commits turns disposable runtimes into robust workflow primitives.
stories.why_read: Learn how to build a versioned filesystem where ephemeral sandboxes commit file changes like atomic database transactions. You will discover how zero-copy branching enables isolated state across automated workflow steps.

stories.title: LLMD unifies open model serving across multiple hardware accelerators
stories.social_post:
Serving modern large language models across heterogeneous hardware typically forces engineering teams to manage fragmented runtimes for NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple silicon.

LLMD addresses this fragmentation by packaging an inference server that supports CUDA, ROCm, TPU, oneAPI, and Metal through a unified runtime. Under the hood, it incorporates critical production serving primitives including continuous batching, paged attention for long contexts, tensor parallelism across devices, and prefix caching to minimize redundant compute.

A particularly interesting capability is native support for DFlash speculative decoding, which delivers up to a tenfold speedup on supported architectures. It also bundles a virtual file system layer to stream weights directly from Hugging Face, S3, or Google Cloud Storage without requiring an explicit local download step.

Standardizing inference primitives across diverse hardware targets significantly reduces infrastructure complexity for machine learning platforms.
stories.why_read: Explore a self-contained runtime for hosting open LLMs across CUDA, ROCm, TPU, and Metal accelerators.

stories.title: Query pushdown in Postgres foreign data wrappers requires negotiation
stories.social_post:
Foreign Data Wrappers (FDWs) are powerful, but their performance hinges on one critical question: how much of a query can you push down to the remote service versus how many rows do you drag back? This is not a simple "send everything" answer.

The ClickHouse team details the intricate "negotiation" involved in pg_clickhouse FDW. They explain that some clauses can be pushed, some require rewriting, and sometimes it is better not to push down specific operations due to unforeseen complexities.

This deep dive reveals the engineering trade-offs when optimizing data transfer and computation across federated systems. It offers invaluable insights for anyone building or operating distributed data architectures.
stories.why_read: Understand the complexities of data pushdown in Postgres Foreign Data Wrappers and why it involves a 'negotiation' between Postgres and remote services rather than simple data transfer.

stories.title: Common replication assumptions underestimate data loss in large clusters
stories.social_post:
Standard durability calculations for replicated storage clusters rely on an assumption that quietly leads to data loss. Engineers often calculate three-way replication risk by multiplying independent disk failure rates, concluding that the chance of triple failure is one in a billion.

That calculation falls apart in large clusters. When a cluster scales to thousands of disks, failure events are not independent. Correlated events like firmware bugs, power anomalies, and simultaneous recovery network saturation happen constantly. More critically, when one disk fails, the rebuild process puts heavy input and output load on the remaining replicas, substantially elevating their probability of failure during the reconstruction window.

Mean time to data loss degrades rapidly as cluster size grows unless partition placement and repair concurrency are strictly bounded. Relying on naive textbook math for storage durability creates an illusion of safety that reality will eventually shatter.

Cluster scale turns rare probabilistic coincidences into operational guarantees.
stories.why_read: Learn why textbook disk failure calculations fail at scale and how correlated recovery failures compromise distributed storage.

stories.title: Why BoxLite is replacing libkrun with a custom VMM
stories.social_post:
Off-the-shelf micro-VM runtimes quickly fall apart when you push them beyond simple sandboxing into production AI agent workloads. When teams embed runtimes like libkrun to provision one micro-VM per agent, they quickly hit low-level virtualization walls that break isolation.

The immediate issue is hardware abstraction limitations. In libkrun, loading guest kernels via shared libraries creates brittle host dependencies, while process terminations swallow error codes and return generic invalid argument errors. Mount more than two virtio directory volumes, and the VM crashes with interrupt request exhaustion because the virtual interrupt table is completely depleted.

Building a custom virtual machine monitor directly against Linux KVM and Apple Hypervisor framework solves these bottlenecks. A purpose-built hypervisor gives developers direct control over device layout, predictable error handling, and sub-millisecond turn resets for stateful agents.

Standard container abstractions often leak state, but purpose-built micro-VM monitors make secure multi-tenant execution practical.
stories.why_read: Discover real-world edge cases with libkrun such as dlopen failures, missing exit statuses, and IRQ exhaustion.

stories.title: Choreography-derived runtime enforcement executes finite multiparty protocols in Rust
stories.social_post:
Writing multi-party distributed protocols usually means maintaining separate state machines for every node and praying that your messages never drift out of sync. Hibana brings choreographic programming to Rust by turning a single global protocol specification into projected runtime state machines for each endpoint.

Unlike traditional implementations that blow up compile times with complex session types, Hibana uses compact runtime descriptors. It operates unconditionally under no_std with zero heap allocations, allowing up to 256 roles to communicate over any transport implementation.

Every send, receive, and routing decision must validate against the projected local program before state progress commits. If an endpoint attempts to execute steps out of order or repeat a message, the runtime kernel rejects the transition immediately.

Choreographic execution eliminates protocol mismatches at the source by deriving node behaviors directly from shared system design.
stories.why_read: Inspect how global multiparty choreographies can be projected into compact local state descriptors in embedded Rust.

stories.title: Projecting global protocol choreography into rust endpoint roles
stories.social_post:
Implementing complex state machines for stateful protocols like QUIC is notoriously bug-prone because coordinating parallel actions across different roles often leads to hidden deadlocks and desynchronization.

Hibana-QUIC takes an unconventional approach by implementing QUIC and HTTP/3 in Rust through choreographic programming. Instead of writing endpoint logic independently, developers declare the global interaction order across roles using choreographic primitives. The compiler then projects this global sequence into per-role state machines, guaranteeing protocol fidelity by construction.

Equally remarkable are the runtime constraints. The entire library operates in no_std mode, strictly forbids unsafe code, and completely avoids heap allocations by refusing to link the alloc crate. Connection endpoints borrow memory arenas and stream slots directly from callers, bounding state execution cleanly.

This design shows how formal protocol choreography and strict systems constraints can combine to make network infrastructure both provably structured and exceptionally predictable under resource pressure.
stories.why_read: Examine how transport state transitions can be statically driven from global protocol choreographies.

stories.title: Building an agent harness from scratch to pass intelligence tests
stories.social_post:
An agent harness is everything surrounding a model that determines whether an autonomous workflow actually functions in production. Stripped down to fundamentals, every agent begins with a simple loop: construct context, issue an inference request to the model, parse tool calls, execute actions, and append outputs back into history.

The real engineering challenge emerges once that loop touches real environments. Production harnesses require strict process sandboxing, deterministic state recovery, and disciplined token pruning. Without explicit boundaries, tool outputs rapidly overflow model context windows, degrade attention spans, and spike execution latency.

Treating the harness as a first-class distributed systems problem matters far more than swapping model checkpoints. When tool failure handlers and context bounds are designed with care, even modest models solve multi-step problems reliably.

A resilient harness turns raw language model calls into dependable software.
stories.why_read: Understand the bare minimum components required to build an iterative loop for tool-calling agents.

stories.title: Megakernels underperform optimized separate kernels during Mac inference
stories.social_post:
Fusing multiple GPU operations into a single megakernel is often treated as the gold standard for squeezing maximum throughput out of unified memory architectures. However, practical profiling on Apple Silicon reveals that this optimization can actually degrade inference performance.

When optimizing a 27-billion-parameter model to hit 200 tokens per second on an M5 Max, an aggressive megakernel implementation ended up 2.7 percent slower than discrete, highly tuned kernels. The root cause comes down to memory bandwidth utilization across asymmetric matrix dimensions.

While streaming probes on the chip reached roughly 570 gigabytes per second and feed-forward gate projections achieved 530 gigabytes per second, narrower down-projections dropped to just 247 gigabytes per second. Removing kernel boundaries inside a fused program does not fix poor memory scheduling for narrower matrix shapes. In fact, it forces underutilized execution blocks to hold resources that discrete kernels manage more cleanly.

Merging kernels blindly cannot compensate for hardware bandwidth bottlenecks.
stories.why_read: Learn why memory bandwidth bottlenecks and narrow matrix shapes prevent fused GPU megakernels from outperforming separate kernels on Apple Silicon.

stories.title: Sandboxed JavaScript programs minimize context overhead from tool calls
stories.social_post:
Sequential tool calling in LLM agent architectures introduces massive context bloat when each intermediate tool response gets dumped back into the prompt window.

Claude Code Mode solves this by shifting tool orchestration into a sandboxed execution environment. Instead of executing multiple round trips across Model Context Protocol servers, the language model generates a single JavaScript script that invokes the tools locally, joins the payloads, and filters the results before returning anything.

The sandboxed Node process runs with strict resource limits, disabling file system access and utilizing Linux network namespaces to prevent unauthorized socket communication. The model receives only the final computed return value rather than megabytes of intermediate JSON dumps.

This architecture protects prompt cache efficiency, minimizes round-trip latency, and drastically reduces token overhead on multi-step workflows.

Treating code execution as the primary integration layer transforms how agents interact with external APIs.
stories.why_read: See how running data transformations in a local sandbox keeps intermediate MCP results out of the LLM context window.

stories.title: Tool-using agent benchmarks fail their advertised executable contracts
stories.social_post:
Most agent benchmarks evaluate model decisions against simulated tools that quietly violate their own interface contracts.

When researchers audited 34 mutating tools across four major agent benchmarks, they confirmed seven tool defects where the underlying code diverged from advertised schemas. In AgentDojo alone, at least 5 out of 25 mutating tools failed to write the state expected by their contracts.

This creates a serious evaluation problem for engineering teams. A model can pick the correct tool and supply valid arguments, yet fail a task because the simulated backend dropped mutations or wrote corrupted state. Even worse, defective tools pass silently because standard benchmark evaluators score final outcomes rather than verifying contract invariants at runtime.

Static analysis caught 14 of 17 confirmed failure sites before executing a single test case. Tracing state provenance showed that multiple benchmark verdicts were derived entirely from state that a broken tool should have written, but never did.

Before you trust leaderboards for tool-calling agents, verify the tools against executable contracts rather than trusting mock implementations.
stories.why_read: Examine how silent defects and violated interface contracts in standard evaluation suites corrupt agent benchmark results.
